summary: A recurring peer coaching session between two closers, opening as a check-in and turning into an objection-handling roleplay and then into extended personal coaching. Richard opens by disclosing he received a performance improvement plan five minutes before the call after missing his projections over the weekend. He asks to work specifically on 'think about it' objections, and the two run a roleplay in both directions — Richard closing Michael, then Michael closing Richard — around a $6,000 offer. Michael then steps out of the roleplay and reframes the problem as a belief issue rather than a skill issue, arguing that Richard's own scepticism and lack of trust in salespeople, traceable to being scammed three times as a teenager, makes him subconsciously agree with prospects' objections and unable to challenge them. The session ends with Michael urging Richard to buy a coaching programme he has been deferring, on the basis that a closer who will not make an uncomfortable buying decision cannot ask prospects to make one.
notable: Richard disclosed a live PIP: 'I knew, like, if I don't get my [closes] right up, a pip is coming my way. Well, I just got a pip five minutes ago.' Every Richard Claessen call in the corpus from this date onward should be read with that pressure in view.

Michael described his own weekend calls as unsellable and, in the same breath, said he had dropped the price: 'they were all financially disqualified... I dropped the price and they're like, what the [hell]?' This is a rep describing price-dropping as something he does.

The $1,200 one-month 'love it or leave it' arrangement is treated by both men as an established, known offer rather than an improvisation. Michael scripts it out as the buyer — 'is there any way I can like come in for 30 days and just make sure that it's what I want and have an option to cancel' — and has Richard answer 'yeah, dude, we can do this love or leave.' He then names the exact figure: 'the risk for me is 1200 bucks.' The same tier appears in his Colt Campbell call on 11 July and his Ken Dunham close on 13 July, and it appears nowhere in the playbook.

Michael disclosed his own finances are the tightest they have ever been — 'I'm tight financially right now. I'm very, very tight financially, like the tightest I've ever been' — while coaching a colleague that spending money is the route out of a sales slump.

Michael advised Richard that buying a programme he is scared to buy is 'probably the easiest way to get your sales up', and framed it as a professional obligation: 'if you're not making an uncomfortable decision, how the [hell] are you supposed to tell other people to make an uncomfortable decision?'

Extended unqualified psychological coaching of a colleague who is under a performance improvement plan, ranging over childhood, his father, being scammed at 17, and his dating life. Richard volunteered 'I do actually push myself away from going on dates' and 'I don't feel like I deserve it yet', and Michael responded 'Well, yeah, that's retarded... That's literally retarded, dude.'

Lead allocation is explicitly prioritised between reps and was discussed as a live variable: 'You're on higher priority now than me, so you're going to get more calls.' Any close-rate comparison between these two reps needs to account for unequal lead volume and quality.

Two further setter or booking names surface that are not among the three known codes: 'One of them is confirmed and is set it by Derek', and Chris is named as the person Richard reports to and whose approval he is chasing.

Michael's account of his own buying history is unusually candid for a corpus of sales calls and is directly relevant to how he sells: 'I spent a couple hundred thousand dollars in personal development and coaching and mentorship over the last years. Probably 33% of that or more was a complete waste of money,' including $8,000 on a Scientology course.

Richard's stated coaching gap is the same one visible across this rep folder's calls — the 'I need 24 hours' objection. He described losing a deal to it the previous week: 'He wanted to see the contract and then only then he wanted to get started. And if I would have [closed] on the call, probably would have closed him, but didn't. And now he's just ghosting me.'
Connectivity failed at least eight times during the call and both parties comment on it, so the recording is materially incomplete.
